Opulent

OP-yoo-lunt -- from Latin opulentus, 'wealthy,' from ops, 'wealth, resources, power': an opulent place is overflowing with resources. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Opulent is overly rich, lavish, or luxurious.

The sultan's palace was so opulent that even the doorknobs were carved from solid gold.

Worked Example

The community center's holiday party, usually just folding chairs and a fruit punch bowl, suddenly featured a chocolate fountain, a live orchestra, and ice sculptures of every guest's initials.

Opulent describes a level of luxury that goes well beyond what's normal or necessary -- a modest community party wouldn't normally have a chocolate fountain and ice sculptures, which is exactly what makes this year's version feel opulent.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

luxurious: extremely comfortable and expensive

lavish: given or spent in extremely generous, showy amounts

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

plain: simple, without decoration

austere: severely simple and stripped of comfort

Where it sits · how far wealth spills into excess — luxurious → opulent → lavish

luxurious vs. opulent: Luxurious describes rich comfort in general, while opulent adds a sense of visible, almost showy display of that wealth.

lavish vs. opulent: Lavish pushes even further than opulent, suggesting an almost excessive, overflowing generosity of spending, not just a rich appearance.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — op-

root — op-: wealth, resources, power (Latin ops)

suffix — -ulent

suffix — -ulent: full of (Latin -ulentus)

Put it together

Put it together: Opulent comes from Latin opulentus, 'wealthy,' from ops, 'wealth, resources, or power' -- something opulent is, at its root, entirely full of resources, the same root behind the word copious.

Use the root in a new word: copious

Use the root in a new word: copious: The chef served copious amounts of fresh bread before the main course even arrived.

Word Choice

Opulent almost always describes places, objects, or lifestyles rather than people directly, and it usually implies visible, showy wealth.
